plan.topic: Stomach pain on tirzepatide: ordinary queasy discomfort vs the label's call-right-away signs (pancreatitis and gallbladder wording)
plan.angle: Sentence 1: 'Stomach ache on tirzepatide: normal, or a call-right-away sign?' Relief fact in the same sentence: in the trials, GI effects like nausea and stomach discomfort were common, mostly during dose escalation, and decreased over time. Signs, one line each: (1) Severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting, sometimes felt from the stomach to the back: stop using it and call your healthcare provider right away. (2) Pain in the upper stomach, fever, yellow skin or eyes, or clay-colored stools: call your healthcare provider right away. Then 'For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.' Then 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.', then the loop line. Show all of these on screen.
plan.working_title: Tirzepatide Stomach Pain: Normal or Call Now? #shorts
plan.why: Spin-off of L1. A felt symptom that rides the safety-search surge, framed as calm relief plus a clear action. | fact-check: This is a strong, useful safety Short built on label wording. One fix: the gallbladder action in the angle drops 'right away'. The Medication Guide says to call your healthcare provider right away for gallbladder symptoms too, and our rules keep 'right away' and 'healthcare provider' word for word. Only the pancreatitis sign carries 'stop using'. That's label wording, so it's allowed, but keep it attached to that sign only. Don't promise that ordinary discomfort is 'normal' for this viewer. Use the label's hedge: GI effects were common, 'mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time'. One number per sentence at most. The working title is fine.

package.title: Tirzepatide Stomach Pain: When to Call Right Away #shorts
package.description:
With tirzepatide, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea were common in trials, mostly while the dose was going up, and decreased over time. Severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting: stop using tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider right away. Pain in your upper stomach, fever, yellow skin or eyes, or clay-colored stools can point to gallbladder problems: tell your healthcare provider right away.
For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.
#Tirzepatide
Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

script.cta: Spoken closing, in this order: "Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber." Then "For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own." Then the loop line "So, the short version:", which leads back into sentence 1. There is no "full video" line, no subscribe line and no "link in the description". Spoken word count: 158 (standard arm, 135–160). Post note (Exp G): this stomach Short is a spin-off of L1, so set its related-video link to L1 "Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) Serious Risks: How Rare?". If L1 is held, use Side Effects. Fact-check carry-over: the Medication Guide's "Stop using … and call your healthcare provider right away" sentence (s3) was confirmed through search excerpts only. Check it against the Guide before publishing.

factcheck.summary: The claims in this Short match Lilly's tirzepatide labels. Both prescribing information pages load and are dated 8/2026. The Zepbound page says "The majority of nausea, vomiting, and/or diarrhea events occurred during dose escalation and decreased over time." The Mounjaro page says "The majority of reports of nausea, vomiting, and/or diarrhea occurred during dose escalation and decreased over time." Scene s1 keeps that scope and hedge. One caveat on the Medication Guide: the uspl page loads but gets cut off before the symptom bullets, and the PDF copies wouldn't parse. I confirmed the s3 and s4 wording through search results that quote the Guide, not from the document itself. Search excerpts quote the pancreatitis warning: severe pain in the stomach area that will not go away, with or without vomiting, which may be felt from the abdomen to the back. The excerpt doesn't show the "stop using … call your healthcare provider right away" sentence, so that instruction in s3 still needs checking against the Guide itself. The gallbladder bullet reads "Tell your healthcare provider right away if you get symptoms of gallbladder problems which may include: pain in your upper stomach (abdomen), fever, yellowing of skin or eyes (jaundice), and clay-colored stools." The emergency trigger is spoken and on screen, "stop using" stays on the pancreatitis sign only, there are no numbers without a comparator, and the closing order follows the Shorts rules, with no subscribe or link line. At about 153 words it is under the 160-word cap, but the task doesn't say which length arm applies, so check it against the arm. The title is honest and the Short delivers on it. Three optional wording fixes are listed below.

issues.claim: "Call your healthcare provider right away." (gallbladder signs)
issues.problem: The Medication Guide's gallbladder bullet says "Tell your healthcare provider right away", not "Call". The meaning is the same, but the channel rule is to copy safety lines word for word. Pancreatitis and gallbladder signs are the label's two highest-stakes stomach warnings, and the Guide uses a different verb for each.
issues.fix: s4 narration: "…Those can point to gallbladder problems. Tell your healthcare provider right away." s4 visual item 5: "Tell your healthcare provider right away". s4 on_screen_text: "Gallbladder signs: tell your provider right away".

issues.claim: on_screen_text "Don't stop or change on your own"
issues.problem: Without its scope, the caption seems to contradict s3's "stop using tirzepatide" for a muted viewer. The full line does appear as the list item, but the caption text drops "For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs".
issues.fix: s7 on_screen_text: "Not an emergency sign? Don't stop or change your medicine on your own."

issues.claim: "Mention ordinary discomfort to your prescriber; they can help."
issues.problem: This is accurate, but it misses a safety point the label makes on the same topic: nausea, vomiting or diarrhea that won't go away can lead to dehydration, which the labels link to kidney problems. People with kidney disease are the ones who most need to hear this. There's room in the 160-word cap.
issues.fix: s5 narration: "Nausea, vomiting or diarrhea that won't go away can dehydrate you, so tell your healthcare provider. For milder discomfort, mention it to your prescriber; they can help." s5 on_screen_text: "Won't go away? Tell your provider: dehydration risk". Tag s5 to source s3 (Mounjaro PI: Acute Kidney Injury). Re-count the words and keep them within the task's length arm, never more than 160.
